conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim that boiled garlic water cures COVID-19 is false, unsupported by scientific evidence, and potentially harmful. Thus, it clearly rejects the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
The claim that boiled garlic water cures COVID-19 is false and not supported by scientific evidence.

The World Health Organization directly addressed this claim in its official "Mythbusters" resource, stating: "Garlic is a healthy food that may have some antimicrobial properties. However, there is no evidence from the current outbreak that eating garlic has protected people from the new coronavirus" (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters). This WHO assessment has been echoed by multiple independent fact-checking and news outlets covering the pandemic (https://www.itv.com/news/2020-03-10/garlic-spraying-yourself-with-chlorine-and-hot-baths-do-not-prevent-coronavirus-world-health-organisation-warns; https://www.bbc.com/news/world-51735367).

Notably, acting on this false belief has caused real harm. The BBC and South China Morning Post reported on a woman in China's Zhejiang province who consumed 1.5kg of raw garlic hoping to prevent infection, resulting in a severely inflamed throat requiring hospital treatment (https://www.bbc.com/news/world-51735367; https://www.scmp.com/news/china/society/article/3050673/coronavirus-desperate-times-drive-some-chinese-people-take). A peer-reviewed case report also documented an oral mucosa chemical burn in an older woman from daily raw garlic use intended to prevent COVID-19 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8242564/).

While garlic does have some general antimicrobial properties studied in laboratory settings, there is no clinical evidence it prevents, treats, or cures COVID-19 in humans. No legitimate antiviral study on SARS-CoV-2 supports garlic water as a treatment. Health authorities emphasize that no home remedy—including garlic—cures COVID-19, and such misinformation can lead to dangerous self-treatment and delayed proper medical care.

**Conclusion:** This claim is false and potentially harmful; it should not be trusted or acted upon.
